extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics interested in fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for using pictorial description and dramatic action in novels — when and how to prepare scenes, manage time, handle recurring characters, shape point of view, and temper romance vs truth. Emphasises practical methods used by Balzac, Dickens, Thackeray, and Stevenson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial impression as preparation for drama
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial impression, wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama—will become an effective agent in the book, instead of remaining the mere decorative introduction that it may seem to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description not as mere decoration but as stored 'reserve of vigour' that prepares and attests the dramatic action which follows; the picture should make the later action plausible and carry part of its force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac was able to pack into a short book—he never wrote a long one—such an effect of crowds and events, above all such an effect of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to compress broad experience into concise narrative without losing emphasis; the pictorial preparation can allow a writer to suggest wide scope in limited pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrent characters must be relevant to the foreground story
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action ... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground. Whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reusing familiar characters across works, ensure any cameo appearances shed irrelevant past associations and serve the immediate story; otherwise they disturb unity and confuse truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed, authoritative setting-description (when warranted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac's minute knowledge lets him reproduce a scene inch by inch, fact by fact, without losing the effect of it as a whole; he offers his impression of the general landscape of the story, a leisurely display which brings us finally to the point of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you present exhaustive detail, it must feel essential and come from an authentic, possessed image of the scene; otherwise such inventory risks being mechanical and telling the reader nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting to temper implausible drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the action ... is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic, it is made to look less so, less hazardous and more real, by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed fantastic or highly romantic elements in a believable background so the contrast is moderated; the pictorial setting can disguise or integrate marvels into credible life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed romance in a background of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If he can get the tale firmly embedded in a background of truth, its falsity may be disguised ... the action would be subdued and kept in its place by the pictorial setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to merge romance and realism via grounding details; if the distinction between the two is too sharp the effect will be false and jarring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual introduction of violent drama through populated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens’s way of dealing with his romantic intrigues was to lead gradually into them, through well-populated scenes of character and humour; so that his world is actual, its air familiar, by the time that his plot begins to thicken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the reader with a lively, believable world before delivering a dramatic climax: populated scenes lend attestation and make sudden or violent drama credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render pictorial effect as scenic action rather than abstract summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens continually holds to the immediate scene ... he is always readier to work in action and dialogue than to describe at large; he is happier in placing a character there before us, as the man or woman talked and behaved in a certain hour, on a certain spot, than in reflecting a long impression of their manner of living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a pictured world, prefer dramatized scenes and evocative incidents over wide generalizing narrative; presenting background through action increases immediacy and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and crystallization of minor characters
rubrics_metrics.description: His opportunities are strictly limited; the author does not help them out by glancing freely into their lives and sketching them broadly ... he is often reduced to the expedient of labelling his people with a trick or a phrase, which they have to bring with them every time they appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When minor characters occupy only a few scenes, render them sharply and economically—use distinctive traits or memorable phrases so they register quickly and reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose point of view to suit the material
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the first person ... is the value of working the drama into a picture, of passing it through a man's thought and catching his reflection of it ... The same method has a different effect, according to the subject upon which it is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select narrative person and viewpoint (first/third, interior/exterior) so that the balance between pictorial impression and dramatic immediacy fits the subject; different POVs will shift the work toward drama or picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey passage of time via prepared scene and routine
rubrics_metrics.description: His preliminary picture included the representation of time, secured the sense of it so thoroughly that there is no necessity for recurring to it again ... The routine of the Maison Grandet is too clearly known to be forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To suggest long durations without extended interior narration, create a scene whose routines and material facts imply the passing years; make the 'sense of time' latent in the world you build so you can summarize elapsed time succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the climax by adequate preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic; that is its task, and that only. It should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction, and nothing need distract it that can be dealt with and despatched at an earlier stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deal with subsidiary material earlier so the climax only needs to supply the necessary final touch; avoid forcing the climax to carry exposition or effects that should have been prepared beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match narrative technique to scarcity of incident (when material is slight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is so little in the way of incident ... it is most puzzling to handle. Balzac makes the episode bulk as largely in the book as it did in her life ... He extends his account of it so far ... that he has written two thirds of the book by the time the young man is finally despatched to the Indies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When external action is sparse, you may either concentrate on interior life or (as Balzac does) expand and dwell on the preparatory episode and build a durable scene so that the few events carry the required weight; choose the method that best sustains the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining iterative or single-subject narratives by heightening intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no development through any variety of incident; it is the same suspense and the same shock, again and again, constantly more disastrous than before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narratives built on repetition (obsession, repeated failures), preserve the straight, sustained movement while increasing intensity and stakes each recurrence rather than relying on incident variety.
